the structure and stability of the siderophore enterohactin is determined by the number of catechol rings, the nature and location of the chelate ring, the length of the peptide backbone, and the nature of the amino acids.
the structure of the iron complex of enterobactine is unique and provides a basis for understanding both its stability and its transport by the ferric enterobactin transporter (FepD/FepC).
In summary, our research is concerned with

the molecular mechanisms by which microorganisms obtain iron from a hostile external environment, the role of iron acquisition in the virulence of microbial pathogens, and the use of siderophores as models for the design of synthetic iron complexing agents.

the molecular recognition of natural and synthetic iron chelators, the synthesis of novel iron chelating agents and their application to the treatment of iron overload, and the development of iron transport systems for use in gene therapy.
the recognition and transport of natural (enterobactin) and synthetic (desferrioxamine B) siderophores by microorganisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the iron complexation and mobilization of siderophores represents one of the most sophisticated and elegant systems for the transport of an essential nutrient in nature.
the siderophore is the most efficient and effective iron complexing agent in nature, and the most efficient mechanism for the mobilization and transport of iron by microorganisms.
iron transport is a complex process that involves a variety of iron complexing agents that have been selected for stability, solubility and bioavailability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structure and function of enterobactine and its analogs are intimately related and that the structure of enterobactins and analogs is a consequence of their biological function.
the stability of the ferric enterobactin complex arises from the unique ability of the catechol groups to form a stable, rigid, six-coordinate, octahedral complex with ferric iron.

we have developed an understanding of the chemistry of the complexation and mobilization of iron by the siderophores, and the structure and function of the siderophore receptors and the transport systems for these molecules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
siderophore-mediated iron transport systems are highly efficient and selective.
enterobactin is not a simple iron chelator but is a highly specific ligand for ferric iron.
the siderophores of bacteria are not only remarkable molecules in their own right, but also provide a model for the design of new chelating agents with potential therapeutic applications in medicine.
